details:
Abandoned, Not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars

What It Does & How It Works Abandoned, Not Forgotten is an interactive web-based storytelling platform and off-world archaeological map that transforms how we view hardware left behind on other worlds—treating landers, rovers, and descent stages not as "space junk," but as historic heritage artifacts. Users can switch between interactive Moon and Mars surface maps featuring authentic NASA planetary projections and click on glowing telemetry beacons to inspect specific mission sites. Each artifact includes a first-person narrative log written from the hardware's perspective, paired with a built-in voice narrator that speaks the machine's story aloud. Users can also explore dedicated tabs covering mission science, orbital reconnaissance verification from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) and Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), space heritage protection laws, and a real-time gallery powered by NASA's open API.

Benefits of the Project

  • Makes complex planetary science and space history engaging, emotional, and accessible to audiences of all ages through interactive visuals and built-in audio narration.
  • Bridges raw NASA open data and authentic planetary coordinates with human-centered storytelling, turning technical telemetry into an intuitive digital museum experience.
  • Serves as an educational resource for students, educators, and space enthusiasts exploring the timeline of robotic and crewed exploration from 1967 to 2024.

Intended Impact This project aims to shift public perception of humanity's footprint across the solar system. By highlighting the ongoing scientific value and historical significance of abandoned equipment, the platform raises awareness about the fragility of off-world historical sites, supports international space heritage frameworks such as the One Small Step to Protect Human Heritage in Space Act, and encourages responsible exploration as humanity returns to the Moon through the Artemis program and prepares for future missions to Mars.

Tools, Coding Languages, Software & Hardware Used

  • Frontend Languages: HTML5, CSS3, and Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+)
  • Software & Version Control: Visual Studio Code, Git, and GitHub (with GitHub Pages for live web hosting)
  • NASA Open Data & APIs: NASA Image and Video Library API (images-api.nasa.gov), NASA Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS) planetary map projections, authentic planetary landing coordinate datasets, and LRO/MRO orbital observation records
  • Browser APIs: Web Speech API (speechSynthesis) for real-time text-to-speech voice narration
  • Hardware: Standard personal computer/laptop for local development and testing

Creativity Rather than presenting a static encyclopedia entry or dry timeline, this project gives defunct spacecraft a voice. Framing historic machines through first-person storytelling—such as the Apollo 11 Eagle descent stage standing motionless in the Sea of Tranquility or Opportunity enduring its final Martian dust storm—creates genuine emotional resonance. Combining real NASA cartographic projections, a chronological jump bar, and instant live API photo lookups with a full-screen lightbox inspector delivers an immersive "Mission Control" experience.

Key Factors Considered

  • Scientific Accuracy & Validity: Every landing coordinate, touchdown date, final transmission date, and orbital proof detail was verified against official NASA mission records to ensure complete factual integrity.
  • Accessibility & User Experience: Designed with a responsive split-screen layout, clear visual telemetry cards, chronological quick-navigation chips, and audio narration so users can explore effortlessly on both desktop and mobile devices.
  • Lightweight & Reliable Architecture: Built cleanly with native web standards and graceful offline fallbacks so the application loads rapidly and handles live NASA API queries smoothly without heavy external dependencies.
